title: Why the Cable in Your Pocket Knots Itself
summary: A translation of the same day's science episode. It explains why an earphone cable in a pocket, or an extension cord in a bag, ties itself in knots when nobody touches it. It starts with the tumbling-box experiment Raymer and Smith published in PNAS in two thousand seven, where about half of the strings longer than one and a half meters knotted within seconds and one hundred twenty different knot types were classified. It then covers the Sumners–Whittington theorem of nineteen eighty-eight, which says the chance of a chain staying unknotted falls to zero exponentially as it grows longer. It ends with why the same mathematics keeps DNA inside the cell under constant threat of knotting, and how topoisomerase enzymes cut those knots apart.
